input:
When a fluid flows over a surface, two spreading processes are at
work at the same time, both arising from the same underlying
molecular mechanism. Momentum spreads outwards from the surface
into the fluid, and heat spreads outwards as well, but the two
processes do not in general proceed at the same rate, and their
relative speed is captured by a dimensionless quantity known as the
Prandtl number. The Prandtl number is defined
as the ratio of the momentum diffusivity to the thermal diffusivity.
To unpack the two terms, momentum diffusivity can be understood as
a measure of how rapidly a difference in velocity spreads through
the fluid and is evened out, while thermal diffusivity similarly
measures how rapidly a difference in temperature spreads through
the fluid and is evened out. Since both diffusivities are
properties of one and the same fluid in one and the same state,
forming their ratio provides a compact way of ordering the two
spreading processes against one another: the number indicates which
process runs ahead, and by how much, independently of the size of
the equipment or the speed of the flow.

In the case where the value is near 1, the two diffusivities are
nearly equal to one another. Momentum and heat consequently spread
at comparable rates, and the velocity boundary layer and the
temperature boundary layer grow to nearly the same thickness. At
any given distance from the surface, the fluid has been set in
motion over roughly the same depth to which it has been heated or
cooled, and neither field can be said to run ahead of the other.

In the contrasting case of a large value, the momentum diffusivity
far exceeds the thermal diffusivity. Momentum spreads readily
whereas heat spreads only slowly, and the velocity boundary layer
grows to a thickness much greater than that of the temperature
boundary layer. Differences in temperature remain confined within
a thin layer against the surface, in fluid that is still moving
well below the free-stream velocity, while differences in velocity
reach much farther out into the flow. Heat transfer at the surface
is then governed by conduction across the thin temperature layer,
and the temperature field near the surface responds only slowly to
any change imposed on it, long after the velocity field has
adjusted itself.
